instincts.title: Physical form dominates performance.
instincts.framing: Logical data types are an abstraction. Every value has a physical byte layout, and that layout, not the logical type, sets the ceiling on scan and compute throughput.

instincts.title: Movement is the cost.
instincts.framing: CPU cycles are cheap relative to moving bytes across copies, processes, disks, and networks. Expert design minimizes and amortizes movement.

instincts.title: Batch beats tuple-at-a-time.
instincts.framing: Per-item overhead from virtual calls, bounds checks, and cache misses dominates when you process one value at a time. Processing batches amortizes that overhead and unlocks SIMD.

instincts.title: Declare what; let the planner choose how.
instincts.framing: You declare intent as SQL or a DataFrame. The engine derives a logical plan, rewrites it, and chooses a physical plan from statistics. Separating what from how is what lets the same query get faster with no rewrite.

instincts.title: The fastest work is skipped work.
instincts.framing: I/O you never issue is free. Layouts and indexes that let the engine prove a chunk is irrelevant beat any amount of faster scanning.

instincts.title: Approximate on purpose.
instincts.framing: Exact answers are often unaffordable and unnecessary. Bounded-error structures give orders-of-magnitude savings for cardinality, quantiles, and similarity.

instincts.title: Placement decides what is cheap.
instincts.framing: In a distributed engine the cost of an operation is set by whether the data it needs is already co-located. Joins and aggregations are cheap when keys are aligned and expensive when they force a shuffle.

instincts.title: Durability is an append-only log plus a snapshot.
instincts.framing: Databases do not overwrite data in place and hope for the best. They append every change to a write-ahead log for durability and keep a snapshot or index for fast reads. Recovery replays the log onto the last snapshot.

instincts.title: Time and ordering are plural and uncertain.
instincts.framing: There is no single notion of when. Event time, ingestion time, and processing time differ, ordering holds only within a partition, and completeness is something you estimate with watermarks rather than know for certain.

instincts.title: Design every pipeline to be safe to re-run.
instincts.framing: Failures, backfills, and replays are normal operations. A pipeline you cannot run twice is a liability. Idempotency, determinism, and explicit history make re-running boring and safe.

instincts.title: A table is metadata over immutable files.
instincts.framing: On object storage there is no in-place update and no atomic rename. A table is a metadata layer that points at a set of immutable files, and a commit swaps metadata rather than data. This is the entire premise of the lakehouse.

instincts.title: Compose interchangeable layers through open standards.
instincts.framing: Modern systems are not monoliths. Storage, catalog, execution engine, and query frontend are separate layers joined by open formats and plan intermediate representations, so each can be swapped independently.

instincts.title: A system that cannot say no will fail.
instincts.framing: Unbounded acceptance leads to collapse. Memory budgets, backpressure, admission control, and scheduling let a system slow or shed work and degrade predictably instead of crashing.

instincts.title: Data is a product with a contract.
instincts.framing: Datasets are products with consumers. Treat them like code: a declared schema, a compatibility policy, data lineage, tests, and an SLA. Verify, do not assume.

instincts.title: Enforce policy at the chokepoint.
instincts.framing: Security enforced in every application drifts and leaks. Enforce policy once at the layer everyone must pass, the catalog or engine, so it is consistent and auditable.

instincts.title: Cost is an architecture decision.
instincts.framing: The cloud bill is a function of design, not an afterthought. Bytes scanned, bytes moved across regions, storage tiering, and the compute purchasing model are all chosen at architecture time.

instincts.title: Meaning becomes geometry.
instincts.framing: Embeddings map meaning into vectors so that semantic similarity becomes distance. Retrieval becomes a geometry problem, and storage and indexing choices follow from that.

instincts.title: Feed the accelerator.
instincts.framing: A GPU starves unless the data pipeline keeps up; the bottleneck is bandwidth, not compute. Training-data systems exist to keep accelerators fed with correct, reproducible data.

nodes.name: Row vs Columnar
nodes.what: Row layout stores all fields of a record together; columnar layout stores each field contiguously. Point lookups favor rows; scans and aggregations favor columns.
nodes.analogy: A row store is a filing cabinet with one folder per customer. A column store is a spreadsheet where each attribute is its own strip you can sum without opening folders.

code.text:
-- columnar engine reads only the 2 columns it needs, not whole rows
SELECT asset_class, sum(market_value) FROM positions GROUP BY asset_class;

nodes.differentiator: Choosing the physical layout per workload, not per habit, is what separates a query that scans a whole table from one that touches two columns. Most teams default to row stores and keep paying for it on every analytical scan.
nodes.decisions: Knowing that scans and aggregations favor columns tells you to land risk positions and trade history in columnar files, while keeping row stores for single-record lookups like a payment status check. The layout choice caps throughput before any tuning begins.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agents that query data repeatedly amplify layout cost, so a columnar store lets a retrieval or analytics step read only the fields it needs and keep per-call latency low. Feature and embedding tables are columnar for exactly this reason.

nodes.name: Encoding Schemes
nodes.what: Dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, bit-packing, and delta encoding shrink columnar data by exploiting repetition and ranges. They run before any general compressor, so the compressor then has less to do.
nodes.analogy: Instead of writing "GBP" a million times, write it once in a legend and store small ticket numbers that point at it.

code.text:
# trades.currency has few distinct values, so a dictionary stores small codes
# pyarrow applies dictionary encoding and bit-packing automatically on Parquet write

nodes.differentiator: Dictionary, run-length, bit-packing, and delta encoding shrink data by exploiting structure the general compressor cannot see, cutting bytes and speeding scans at once. Teams that pick encodings deliberately get smaller files and faster filters than those who accept engine defaults.
nodes.decisions: Choosing encodings to match a column, dictionary for currency codes or delta for timestamps, decides how cheaply a risk report scans years of trades. It turns storage layout into a lever on query cost rather than an afterthought.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature and embedding tables are scanned constantly by training and retrieval, so well-encoded columns lower the bytes each agent step must move. Predicate-friendly encodings also let a retrieval filter skip data instead of decoding it.

nodes.name: Compression Codecs
nodes.what: Snappy, LZ4, ZSTD, and gzip trade CPU cycles for fewer bytes moved. The right pick depends on whether the workload is I/O bound or CPU bound.
nodes.analogy: Vacuum-packing luggage. Tighter packing saves cargo space but costs time at both ends.

code.text:
# ZSTD for cold, rarely read data; Snappy for hot, frequently scanned data
df.write.option("compression", "zstd").parquet(path)

nodes.differentiator: Snappy, LZ4, ZSTD, and gzip trade CPU for fewer bytes, and the right pick depends on whether the job is I/O bound or CPU bound. Choosing per dataset, not globally, is what keeps both storage bills and scan times down.
nodes.decisions: Matching codec to access pattern, ZSTD for cold claims archives and Snappy for hot surveillance scans, sets the cost and latency of every read. It is a deliberate tradeoff, not a default.
nodes.ai_agentic: High-throughput training reads favor light, fast codecs so the GPU is never starved waiting on decompression. Cold vector and feature history can use heavier codecs since it is read rarely.

nodes.name: Apache Arrow
nodes.what: Apache Arrow is a language-agnostic in-memory columnar layout standard. A shared format lets engines and libraries pass data without re-serializing it.
nodes.analogy: A common shipping pallet size. Any forklift in any warehouse can move it without repacking.
ideas: the file and row group and page hierarchy

code.text:
import pyarrow as pa
t = pa.table({"trade_id": [1, 2], "price": [99.5, 100.0]})  # shareable, no recopy

nodes.differentiator: Arrow is a shared in-memory columnar standard, so engines and libraries pass data without re-serializing it. Standardizing on it removes the copy-and-parse tax that quietly dominates multi-tool pipelines.
nodes.decisions: Building a pipeline around Arrow lets Spark, Polars, and pandas hand off risk or claims data with no per-row conversion, deciding whether a stage costs seconds or minutes. It makes tool choice a per-step decision rather than a lock-in.
nodes.ai_agentic: Model serving and retrieval stacks move feature batches between processes constantly, and Arrow lets them share memory instead of copying. That keeps agent tool-calls that fetch data cheap and low-latency.

nodes.name: Copies and SerDe
nodes.what: Every boundary at the operating system, process, and runtime level can force a buffer copy. Converting between formats, called SerDe, is often the largest single cost in a pipeline.
nodes.analogy: Each time a parcel changes courier it gets unpacked and repacked. The repacking, not the driving, eats the day.

code.text:
# avoid: df.toPandas() then rebuilding a Spark frame forces a full SerDe round trip
# prefer: stay in one engine, or hand off through Arrow

nodes.differentiator: Serialization between engines is often the hidden majority of a pipeline's cost, invisible in the query plan. Engineers who count SerDe boundaries, not just compute, find the real bottleneck.
nodes.decisions: Knowing that a toPandas round trip forces a full SerDe pass tells you to stay in one engine or hand off through Arrow. That single choice can dominate the runtime of a nightly reserving job.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agent pipelines chain many tools, and each naive handoff re-serializes the payload, adding latency and cost per step. Minimizing copies is what keeps a multi-tool retrieval chain responsive.

nodes.name: Zero-Copy
nodes.what: mmap, shared memory, and Arrow IPC let two consumers read the same bytes with no copy. The fastest copy is the one you never make.
nodes.analogy: Two people reading one whiteboard instead of each transcribing it into a notebook.

code.text:
import pyarrow as pa
buf = pa.memory_map("trades.arrow")  # read without copying into the heap

nodes.differentiator: Zero-copy shares a buffer by reference instead of duplicating it, so large datasets move between components at pointer speed. It is the difference between passing a position book and photocopying it.
nodes.decisions: Designing for zero-copy handoffs decides whether a large exposure dataset can be shared across steps without exhausting the memory budget. It turns data movement from a cost into a near-free operation.
nodes.ai_agentic: Loading training batches and retrieved context repeatedly makes copy cost add up fast, so zero-copy paths keep GPUs fed and retrieval latency flat. It is a core reason Arrow-based stacks scale.

nodes.name: The Shuffle
nodes.what: A shuffle redistributes rows across the cluster by key so all rows with the same key meet. It writes to disk, transfers over the network, and reads back, which makes it the most expensive distributed operation.
nodes.analogy: Telling a stadium crowd to re-seat themselves by birth month. Everyone moves at once and the aisles jam.

code.text: df.groupBy("customer_id").sum("amount")  # triggers a shuffle on customer_id

nodes.differentiator: The shuffle, the all-to-all exchange behind joins and group-bys, is usually the most expensive step in a distributed job. Understanding when one is triggered separates a tuned pipeline from a slow one.
nodes.decisions: Recognizing that a wide aggregation forces a shuffle tells you to pre-partition or pre-aggregate exposure data before it explodes across the network. Avoiding a needless shuffle can cut a job's cost by an order of magnitude.
nodes.ai_agentic: Large-scale feature computation and dataset preparation are shuffle-heavy, so shuffle awareness governs the cost of building training data. Cutting shuffles is often the biggest lever on pipeline spend.

nodes.name: Columnar Transport
nodes.what: Arrow Flight and Flight SQL move columnar batches over the wire without row-by-row encoding. This removes SerDe from the network path.
nodes.analogy: Shipping a pre-loaded container instead of handing over boxes one at a time at the dock.

code.text:
# a Flight SQL client receives Arrow batches directly, with no per-row parse
# client.execute("SELECT * FROM trades").read_all()

nodes.differentiator: Columnar transport such as Arrow Flight ships column batches over the wire with no per-row parsing at either end. It removes the row-by-row decode that throttles conventional database clients.
nodes.decisions: Choosing a columnar transport for moving market data to an analytics client decides whether results arrive in one batch or trickle row by row. It makes bulk data movement a first-class, fast operation.
nodes.ai_agentic: Serving features and retrieved rows to models benefits from columnar transport because batches arrive ready to vectorize. It keeps the data path to inference short and parse-free.

nodes.name: Volcano Model
nodes.what: The classic Volcano model iterator pulls one tuple at a time through a tree of operators. It is simple and composable, but the per-tuple function-call overhead is large.
nodes.analogy: Passing one brick at a time down a line of workers, each pausing to receive and hand off.

code.text: # conceptual: for row in child.next(): emit(predicate(row))  # one call per row

nodes.differentiator: The Volcano model processes one row per operator call, which is simple but pays a function-call and cache cost on every tuple. Knowing it is the baseline explains why vectorized and compiled engines are faster.
nodes.decisions: Recognizing tuple-at-a-time execution as the bottleneck tells you when to move a hot reporting query onto a vectorized engine. It frames a concrete upgrade path rather than blind tuning.
nodes.ai_agentic: Data preparation for models runs over huge row counts, where per-row overhead is ruinous, so the Volcano model marks what to avoid at scale. It is the contrast that motivates batch-oriented processing.

nodes.name: Vectorized Execution
nodes.what: Operators process batches of values, for example 1024 at a time, so the CPU runs tight loops and SIMD instructions. This amortizes dispatch cost across the whole batch.
nodes.analogy: Stamping a whole sheet of forms in one press rather than one form per pull of the lever.

code.text:
import polars as pl
pl.scan_parquet("trades.parquet").filter(pl.col("price") > 100).collect()  # batched

nodes.differentiator: Vectorized execution processes columns in batches so the CPU can use SIMD and stay cache-friendly, often several times faster than row-at-a-time. Choosing a vectorized engine is a throughput decision made before any query tuning.
nodes.decisions: Running scans and aggregations on a vectorized engine decides how quickly a firm can recompute exposures or surveillance metrics over billions of rows. It sets the performance ceiling for analytical work.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature transforms and embedding preprocessing are column-heavy and map naturally onto vectorized execution, keeping data pipelines ahead of the model. It is why modern data-for-AI stacks are columnar and batched.

nodes.name: Code Generation
nodes.what: Whole-stage code generation and JIT compile a query fragment into specialized machine code. It removes interpreter overhead and is used by Photon, DuckDB, and Velox.
nodes.analogy: Casting a custom tool for one job instead of reaching for a general adjustable wrench on every turn.

code.text:
# Spark fuses filter, project, and aggregate into one generated function
# inspect with df.explain(mode="codegen")

nodes.differentiator: Code generation fuses several query operators into one compiled function, removing interpreter overhead between steps. It lets an engine run a filter, project, and aggregate as a single tight loop.
nodes.decisions: Knowing an engine can fuse operators tells you a complex reporting expression may cost far less than its number of steps suggests. It changes how you reason about query cost.
nodes.ai_agentic: Fused pipelines cut the per-record overhead of preparing large training and feature sets, so more of the budget goes to useful work. It compounds across the massive row counts AI workloads demand.

nodes.name: Three Plan Levels
nodes.what: A query exists at three levels: the logical plan (what), the physical plan (how, with chosen operators), and the DAG of distributed tasks that actually runs. An expert can point to any one of the three on demand.
nodes.analogy: A trip is a destination, then a chosen route and transport, then the turn-by-turn legs you drive.

code.text:
EXPLAIN
SELECT c.country, sum(p.amount)
FROM payments p JOIN customers c USING(customer_id)
GROUP BY 1;

nodes.differentiator: Separating logical, optimized, and physical plans lets the engine reason about what to compute apart from how, so one query can run many ways. Understanding the levels is what lets an engineer read and trust a plan.
nodes.decisions: Reading the physical plan shows whether a risk query will broadcast, shuffle, or over-scan before it runs for an hour. It turns performance from guesswork into inspection.
nodes.ai_agentic: When an agent or LLM emits a query, the plan levels are where you verify it does the intended, bounded work. They give a checkable artifact between a generated query and its execution.

nodes.name: Lazy vs Eager
nodes.what: Lazy engines such as Spark, Polars, and Dask build the full plan before executing and optimize across the whole query. Eager engines such as pandas run each step at once and cannot reorder.
nodes.analogy: A chef reading the whole recipe before starting versus shopping for each ingredient mid-cook.

code.text:
import polars as pl
q = pl.scan_parquet("payments.parquet").filter(pl.col("amount") > 1e6)  # nothing runs
q.collect()  # plan is optimized, then executed

nodes.differentiator: Lazy evaluation defers work until a result is demanded, letting the optimizer see the whole computation and prune it, unlike eager step-by-step execution. That global view is where most automatic savings come from.
nodes.decisions: Building a reserving pipeline lazily lets the engine fold filters and projections together instead of materializing every intermediate. It decides whether a chain of transforms is cheap or wasteful.
nodes.ai_agentic: Lazy feature pipelines let the engine push filters down before any data is read, keeping training-set builds efficient. Deferred execution is what makes large, composable data-for-AI pipelines affordable.

nodes.name: Rule-Based Optimization
nodes.what: Mechanical rewrites that are always safe: predicate pushdown, projection pushdown, constant folding. They shrink the work before any cost is considered.
nodes.analogy: Crossing items off a shopping list that you already have at home before driving to the store.

code.text: # WHERE amount > 1e6 is pushed into the Parquet scan; non-matching row groups are skipped

nodes.differentiator: Rule-based optimization applies always-safe rewrites like predicate pushdown and projection pruning that shrink work regardless of data. These wins are free and deterministic, the baseline every engine should capture.
nodes.decisions: Trusting that a filter will be pushed into the Parquet scan tells you to write queries plainly and let the optimizer skip row groups. It lets you reason about cost from the rules rather than the syntax.
nodes.ai_agentic: Deterministic rewrites make generated queries safer, since a pushed-down filter behaves the same every run. That predictability matters when an agent, not a person, is authoring the query.

nodes.name: Cost-Based Optimization
nodes.what: Using table statistics such as row counts, number of distinct values, and histograms to choose join order, join algorithm, and physical operators by estimated cost. The optimizer is only as good as the statistics it is given.
nodes.analogy: A navigation app picking a route from live traffic estimates rather than always taking the straightest line.
ideas: optimization criteria such as latency versus shuffle bytes

code.text: ANALYZE TABLE trades COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS instrument_id;  -- feeds the cost model

nodes.differentiator: Cost-based optimization uses statistics to choose among valid plans, picking join orders a rule set cannot. Its quality is only as good as the statistics behind it, which is where teams win or lose.
nodes.decisions: Keeping table statistics fresh lets the optimizer pick the right join order for a multi-table exposure query instead of a catastrophic one. Maintaining stats is a deliberate operational decision, not automatic.
nodes.ai_agentic: Retrieval and feature joins over large tables depend on good plans, so stale statistics quietly inflate every AI data pipeline. Cost-based choices keep those joins from degrading as data grows.

nodes.name: Adaptive Query Execution
nodes.what: Adaptive query execution replans mid-flight using real runtime statistics. For example it switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast join once it sees the true build-side size.
nodes.analogy: Re-routing your drive after you actually hit the jam, not just from the morning forecast.

code.text: spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")  # coalesce partitions, fix skew at runtime

nodes.differentiator: Adaptive execution re-plans mid-query using real runtime statistics, fixing bad estimates that static planning cannot. It shines exactly where data is skewed or poorly estimated, which is common in real workloads.
nodes.decisions: Enabling adaptive execution lets a join on skewed counterparty data recover at runtime instead of stalling on one partition. It reduces the need to hand-tune every problem query.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature and retrieval joins over uneven real-world distributions benefit from runtime re-planning, keeping large data-prep jobs from hanging on hot keys. It adds resilience to pipelines that feed models.

nodes.name: Data Skipping
nodes.what: Min and max zone maps and bloom filters stored per file or block let the engine skip data that cannot match a predicate. This avoids I/O entirely rather than scanning faster.
nodes.analogy: A library catalog telling you a wing holds no books in your subject, so you never walk in.

code.text: -- row-group min and max on trade_ts let WHERE trade_ts >= DATE '2025-01-01' skip old groups

nodes.differentiator: Data skipping uses per-file min/max stats and zone maps to avoid reading files that cannot match a filter. The fastest scan is the one that never opens the file, and skipping is how you get it.
nodes.decisions: Clustering data so filters prune whole files decides whether a query for one trading desk reads gigabytes or terabytes. It converts a filter into a physical read reduction.
nodes.ai_agentic: Retrieval and feature lookups filtered by time or entity can skip most of a table when stats are maintained, keeping per-call latency low. Skipping is what makes point-in-time reads over huge histories practical.

nodes.name: Pushdown
nodes.what: Pushing predicates, projections, aggregates, limits, and even joins down into the storage layer or remote source. Less data is read and transferred as a result.
nodes.analogy: Asking the warehouse to ship only the red size-10 shoes instead of shipping everything and sorting at home.

code.text: spark.read.parquet(path).select("trade_id", "price").filter("venue = 'LSE'")  # both pushed

nodes.differentiator: Pushdown moves filters, projections, and aggregations down to the storage or source layer so less data ever moves up. It attacks cost at the earliest possible point in the pipeline.
nodes.decisions: Pushing a date and desk filter into the scan means a report touches only the relevant slice of a position history. It is often the single largest determinant of query cost.
nodes.ai_agentic: Pushing predicates into vector and feature stores keeps retrieved sets small and relevant, controlling both latency and downstream context size. It is essential when an agent issues many data calls.

nodes.name: Partitioning Strategies
nodes.what: Hash partitioning, range partitioning, and round-robin partitioning decide how rows map to partitions. The right choice aligns physical placement with the query's filter and join keys.
nodes.analogy: Filing invoices by month, which is range, versus by client initial, which is hash, depending on how you search them.

code.text: df.write.partitionBy("trade_date").parquet(path)  # filters on trade_date prune directories

nodes.differentiator: Partitioning lays data out by a key so queries prune irrelevant partitions, but the wrong key creates tiny files or skew. Choosing the partition column well is one of the highest-leverage layout decisions.
nodes.decisions: Partitioning trades by date and asset class lets surveillance and reporting read only what they need, while a bad choice forces full scans. The decision shapes every query that follows.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature and event tables partitioned by time and entity make point-in-time and incremental reads cheap for training and retrieval. Good partitioning keeps AI data pipelines from re-reading history.

nodes.name: Bucketing and Clustering
nodes.what: Persisting a partitioning or sort order to storage so future queries skip the shuffle or skip files. Clustering co-locates related rows physically.
nodes.analogy: Pre-sorting the mailroom shelves so the daily delivery never has to be re-sorted.

code.text: df.write.bucketBy(64, "customer_id").sortBy("customer_id").saveAsTable("payments_bucketed")

nodes.differentiator: Bucketing and clustering co-locate rows by key so joins and lookups avoid shuffles and read less. They tune the physical layout for the access pattern rather than the logical schema.
nodes.decisions: Bucketing two large tables on the same key lets a counterparty join proceed without a shuffle, a decision that can dominate join cost. It is layout chosen for the queries you actually run.
nodes.ai_agentic: Clustering feature tables on the retrieval join key keeps lookups local and fast under heavy query volume. It stabilizes latency as the number of agent-driven reads grows.

nodes.name: Sketches
nodes.what: Compact probabilistic summaries: HyperLogLog for distinct counts, t-digest for quantiles, Count-Min sketch for frequencies. They use constant memory, are mergeable, and have bounded error.
nodes.analogy: Estimating crowd size from one sampled section rather than counting every head.

code.text: SELECT approx_count_distinct(customer_id) FROM payments;  -- HyperLogLog under the hood

nodes.differentiator: Sketches like HyperLogLog and t-digest answer count-distinct and quantile questions in tiny, mergeable state with bounded error. They trade exactness for orders-of-magnitude less memory, often an easy trade.
nodes.decisions: Using a sketch for distinct counterparties or approximate exposure percentiles gives a good-enough answer in real time instead of an expensive exact pass. It lets you decide when approximate is sufficient.
nodes.ai_agentic: Sketches make cheap, streaming monitors for data drift and cardinality that agents and pipelines can consult continuously. Bounded-error summaries are ideal for always-on observability.

nodes.name: ANN Tradeoff
nodes.what: Approximate nearest neighbor search trades a little recall for large latency gains. Every vector index exposes a recall, latency, and build-cost triangle.
nodes.analogy: Asking a few well-connected locals for the nearest cafe instead of measuring the distance to every cafe in the city.

code.text:
# HNSW: a higher ef_search raises recall and latency together
# index.search(query_vec, k=10, ef_search=128)

nodes.differentiator: Exact nearest-neighbor search does not scale to millions of vectors, so approximate search trades a controllable slice of recall for far lower latency. Engineers who tune that knob rather than accept a library default own the accuracy versus cost frontier.
nodes.decisions: Setting recall targets explicitly lets you decide, for a fraud or sanctions-screening lookup, how much missed-match risk is acceptable at a given latency budget. The same index can serve a compliance query and a product query at different operating points.
nodes.ai_agentic: Approximate search is the retrieval core of RAG and agent memory, so its recall setting bounds how often an agent sees the right context. Under-tuned recall surfaces downstream as confident but unsupported answers.

nodes.name: Learned Indexes
nodes.what: Replacing a traditional index with a model that predicts the storage position of a key. It works when the key distribution is learnable.
nodes.analogy: Guessing a word's page in a dictionary from its first letter instead of binary searching every time.

code.text: # model maps key -> approximate offset, then a small local search corrects the guess

nodes.differentiator: A learned index models the key-to-position mapping and corrects with a small local search, replacing parts of a traditional structure. It is a reminder that an index is a predictor, and predictors can be learned.
nodes.decisions: Considering a learned index for a stable, sorted key lets you weigh memory and lookup cost against a classic B-tree. It broadens the design space for hot lookups.
nodes.ai_agentic: Learned structures show how model-driven components can sit inside the data layer itself, blurring the line between index and inference. They preview data systems that adapt their own access paths.

nodes.name: Narrow vs Wide Dependencies
nodes.what: Narrow dependencies such as map and filter need no data movement. Wide dependencies such as group-by and joins on unaligned keys require a shuffle, and that boundary defines stage boundaries.
nodes.analogy: Narrow is each worker finishing their own pile. Wide is everyone stopping to swap piles by category.

code.text:
df.filter("amount > 1e6")        # narrow, no shuffle
df.groupBy("account_id").count() # wide, shuffle

nodes.differentiator: Narrow dependencies keep each partition's work local, while wide dependencies force a shuffle across the cluster. Knowing which transforms are wide predicts where a job will get expensive.
nodes.decisions: Structuring a pipeline to keep transforms narrow until a single, necessary wide step decides its network cost. It lets you place the expensive boundary on purpose.
nodes.ai_agentic: Building large training sets means sequencing narrow maps and minimizing wide exchanges to keep costs bounded. Dependency shape is a primary lever on data-prep spend.

nodes.name: Distributed Joins
nodes.what: Broadcast join ships a small table to every node; shuffle hash join repartitions both sides by key; sort-merge join sorts both sides. Size and skew pick the winner.
nodes.analogy: Broadcast hands everyone a pocket reference. Shuffle re-seats both groups by key. Sort-merge lines both up in order and walks them together.

code.text:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
trades.join(broadcast(instruments), "instrument_id")  # ship the small dimension everywhere

nodes.differentiator: Distributed joins come in strategies, broadcast, shuffle-hash, sort-merge, each with a different cost profile by table size and skew. Picking the right one is often the whole performance story of a job.
nodes.decisions: Matching join strategy to the data, broadcasting a small reference table against a huge position book, decides whether a join is seconds or hours. It is a deliberate, size-aware choice.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature and retrieval joins over large tables live or die on join strategy, so understanding it keeps AI data pipelines from stalling. It governs the cost of assembling model inputs.

nodes.name: Broadcast vs Shuffle
nodes.what: The deciding factors are the build-side size estimate, selectivity, and skew. A wrong estimate turns a cheap broadcast join into an out-of-memory failure or forces a needless shuffle.
nodes.analogy: Deciding whether to mail everyone a copy or call a central meeting depends on how big the document is.

code.text: spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 10 * 1024 * 1024)  # 10 MB cutoff

nodes.differentiator: Broadcasting ships a small table to every node to avoid a shuffle; a shuffle join redistributes both sides. Choosing between them by size is a simple decision with outsized impact.
nodes.decisions: Broadcasting a small rating table against a large trade set avoids a costly exchange, while broadcasting something too big exhausts memory. Getting the threshold right is the decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Joining a compact lookup against a large feature table at retrieval time favors broadcast to keep latency low. The choice recurs constantly in AI data assembly.

nodes.name: Skew and Salting
nodes.what: Skew is when a few keys hold most of the rows and overload one task. Salting splits hot keys across tasks, and adaptive query execution can detect and split skewed partitions.
nodes.analogy: One checkout lane jammed because everyone buys the same item, so you open extra lanes just for that item.

code.text:
from pyspark.sql.functions import concat_ws, rand
# spread a hot customer_id across 8 sub-keys, join, then aggregate the salt away
df.withColumn("k_salt", concat_ws("_", "customer_id", (rand() * 8).cast("int")))

nodes.differentiator: Skew, where one key holds most of the rows, stalls a job on a single overloaded task, and salting spreads that key across sub-keys. Handling skew keeps a distributed job from being bottlenecked by one hot value.
nodes.decisions: Salting a dominant customer or issuer key lets a join finish evenly instead of waiting on one straggler partition. It is a targeted fix for a specific, common failure.
nodes.ai_agentic: Real entity distributions are heavily skewed, so feature joins over popular entities need salting to stay balanced. It prevents one hot entity from dominating a training-set build.

nodes.name: Spilling
nodes.what: When an operator exceeds its memory budget it spills to disk and continues, trading speed for completion. Spill-aware operators degrade gracefully instead of failing.
nodes.analogy: Running out of desk space and stacking overflow papers on the floor rather than stopping work.

code.text:
# external sort writes sorted runs to disk then merges them
# spill bytes show up in the Spark UI stage metrics

nodes.differentiator: Spilling writes intermediate data to disk when it exceeds memory, trading speed for the ability to finish at all. Understanding spill is how you tell a healthy job from one thrashing on disk.
nodes.decisions: Watching spill metrics tells you whether to raise memory, reduce partition size, or restructure a heavy aggregation on exposure data. It turns out-of-memory guesswork into a measured tuning loop.
nodes.ai_agentic: Large shuffles and sorts in data-prep spill under pressure, so spill visibility keeps AI pipeline costs and runtimes predictable. It is a key signal when scaling feature computation.

nodes.name: Write-Ahead Log
nodes.what: Every change is appended to a write-ahead log and flushed before the data pages change. A crash is recovered by replaying the log, which makes the log the foundational durability primitive.
nodes.analogy: Writing your move in a notebook before you move the piece, so an interrupted game can resume exactly.

code.text:
# append the change record, fsync, then mutate pages; replay the log on restart
# a payment insert is durable once its log record is flushed

nodes.differentiator: A write-ahead log makes a change durable by appending and flushing the intent before mutating state, so a crash can replay to a consistent point. It is the mechanism behind the promise that a committed payment is not lost.
nodes.decisions: Relying on WAL semantics tells you when a write is truly durable and safe to acknowledge, which is central to any financial system of record. It defines the boundary of a committed transaction.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agentic systems that take actions need a durable, replayable record of what was done for recovery and audit. The WAL pattern is how you make an action log trustworthy after failure.

nodes.name: B-Tree
nodes.what: The workhorse OLTP index: balanced and sorted, strong for point lookups and range scans, updated in place. It is the default index behind most relational engines.
nodes.analogy: A library index with sorted tabs you binary-search instead of walking every shelf.

code.text: CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_id ON accounts(account_id);  -- B-tree for point lookups and ranges

nodes.differentiator: B-trees keep data sorted for fast point lookups and range scans and are the default for read-heavy, update-in-place workloads. Knowing their strengths frames when they beat log-structured stores.
nodes.decisions: Choosing a B-tree index for frequent single-record lookups, like fetching a customer's current status, matches structure to access. It is a read-optimized decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Serving current-state features and metadata for models benefits from B-tree point lookups. It is the right structure when reads dominate and updates are in place.

nodes.name: LSM Tree
nodes.what: Writes buffer in an in-memory memtable, flush to sorted SSTables, and merge through compaction. This design dominates write-heavy systems because writes are sequential.
nodes.analogy: Jotting notes on sticky pads, then periodically filing them in sorted order.

code.text:
# writes land in a memtable, flush to immutable SSTables, compaction merges and sorts
# suits high-rate trade capture and surveillance event stores

nodes.differentiator: LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted files that compaction later merges, favoring high write rates over in-place updates. They are built for ingest-heavy stores like trade capture.
nodes.decisions: Choosing an LSM store for a high-rate surveillance or event stream matches structure to a write-dominated load. It trades some read amplification for sustained ingest.
nodes.ai_agentic: High-volume event and interaction logs that feed models fit LSM write patterns well. It is the structure behind stores that must absorb continuous, fast writes.

nodes.name: MVCC
nodes.what: Multi-version concurrency control lets readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions. Readers and writers do not block each other.
nodes.analogy: Each reader gets a photocopy of the ledger as of the moment they started reading.

code.text:
-- a long report reads a consistent snapshot while new trades keep arriving
SELECT count(*) FROM trades;  -- sees the data as of statement start

nodes.differentiator: MVCC gives each reader a consistent snapshot by versioning rows, so reads never block writes and vice versa. It is what lets a long analytical query run correctly while updates continue.
nodes.decisions: Relying on snapshot isolation lets a reserving report read a stable view of claims while new claims land, without locking. It decides how concurrency and correctness coexist.
nodes.ai_agentic: Reproducible training and retrieval need a stable snapshot of data as of a version, which MVCC provides. Versioned reads are what make an AI result traceable to exact inputs.

nodes.name: Copy-on-Write vs Merge-on-Read
nodes.what: Copy-on-write rewrites whole files on update, which is read-fast and write-heavy. Merge-on-read writes small deltas merged at read time, which is write-fast and read-heavier. The same tradeoff reappears in lakehouse formats.
nodes.analogy: Re-typing the whole document on every edit versus keeping a list of edits applied only when someone reads it.

code.text:
# copy-on-write rewrites the data file; merge-on-read appends a delta merged on read
# revised reinsurance claims favor merge-on-read for cheap frequent updates

nodes.differentiator: Copy-on-write rewrites files on update for fast reads; merge-on-read appends deltas merged at query time for fast writes. The choice tunes a table for its read/write balance.
nodes.decisions: Frequently revised reinsurance claims favor merge-on-read for cheap updates, while read-heavy reference data favors copy-on-write. It is a per-table decision about where to pay the cost.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature tables with frequent corrections lean merge-on-read, while stable embedding tables lean copy-on-write for fast retrieval. Matching the mode to update rate keeps AI reads cheap.

nodes.name: Event Time vs Processing Time
nodes.what: Event time is when something happened, ingestion time is when it arrived, and processing time is when the engine handled it. Late and out-of-order data make the three diverge.
nodes.analogy: A postcard carries the date it was written, the postmark date, and the day you finally read it.
nodes.example_note: Reinsurance fits well: loss_date is event time, report_date is ingestion time

code.text:
-- claims can be reported years after the loss occurs
SELECT date_trunc('year', loss_date) AS yr, count(*) FROM claims GROUP BY 1;

nodes.differentiator: Event time is when something happened; processing time is when the system saw it, and they diverge under delay. Treating them as distinct is the foundation of correct time-based analytics.
nodes.decisions: Aggregating trades by event time, not arrival time, is what makes a daily risk cut correct despite late-arriving data. Conflating the two silently corrupts every time window.
nodes.ai_agentic: Features and labels must be computed on event time to avoid leakage from data that arrived later. The distinction is central to honest, point-in-time model inputs.

nodes.name: Watermarks
nodes.what: A watermark is the engine's estimate that no events older than time T will still arrive, which lets it close a window. Completeness is therefore a bet, not a certainty.
nodes.analogy: Closing the ballot box at a deadline, accepting that a few late votes may be lost.

code.text: events.withWatermark("trade_ts", "10 minutes").groupBy(window("trade_ts", "1 minute")).count()

nodes.differentiator: A watermark is the stream's estimate that event time has advanced past a point, letting it decide when a window is complete. It is how a streaming system reasons about lateness without waiting forever.
nodes.decisions: Setting a watermark trades result latency against how much late data you tolerate, a concrete choice for near-real-time surveillance. It defines when a windowed metric is safe to emit.
nodes.ai_agentic: Streaming feature pipelines use watermarks to decide when a feature value is final for a timestamp. It keeps online features consistent with their eventual offline values.

nodes.name: Windowing
nodes.what: Tumbling, sliding, and session windows cut an unbounded stream into finite chunks to aggregate. The window type encodes the business question.
nodes.analogy: Counting traffic per fixed hour, per rolling hour, or per gap-separated rush.

code.text:
from pyspark.sql.functions import window
payments.groupBy(window("payment_ts", "1 minute")).sum("amount")  # tumbling 1-minute windows

nodes.differentiator: Windowing groups an unbounded stream into bounded tumbling, sliding, or session windows so aggregation is possible. The window choice defines what a streaming metric actually measures.
nodes.decisions: Choosing a sliding versus session window changes whether an alerting metric on trading activity reflects a fixed interval or a burst of behavior. It shapes the meaning of the result.
nodes.ai_agentic: Real-time features are almost always windowed aggregates, so window definitions directly determine feature semantics for online models. Getting them right keeps online and offline features aligned.

nodes.name: Ordering Guarantees
nodes.what: Ordering holds within a partition but not across partitions, and global order costs coordination. The partition key decides what stays ordered.
nodes.analogy: Each checkout line is ordered, but there is no single order across all the lines.
ideas: wall-clock versus logical clocks versus hybrid logical clocks

code.text:
# Kafka preserves order within a partition keyed by account_id, not across partitions
# choose the partition key so per-account events stay ordered

nodes.differentiator: Message systems guarantee order only within a partition, not across them, and the partition key decides what stays ordered. Knowing this prevents assuming a global order that does not exist.
nodes.decisions: Keying a stream by account so per-account events stay ordered decides whether downstream state is correct. The partition key is a correctness decision, not just a scaling one.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agent memory and event-sourced state depend on correct per-entity ordering to reconstruct history faithfully. Choosing the key that preserves the order you rely on is essential.

nodes.name: Idempotency and Determinism
nodes.what: Idempotent writes produce the same end state on re-run; deterministic transforms produce the same output for the same input. Together with replayability they make recovery safe.
nodes.analogy: A switch set to on lands in the same state no matter how many times you push it toward on.
nodes.differentiator: Idempotent, deterministic steps produce the same result no matter how many times they run, which is what makes a pipeline safe to retry. Without it, a re-run can double-count or diverge.
nodes.decisions: Designing an ingestion step to be idempotent means a failed batch can be safely replayed without double-booking a payment or claim. It is the property that makes recovery trustworthy.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agents retry and re-run tools, so idempotent, deterministic operations keep repeated actions from compounding into errors. Determinism also makes agent behavior auditable and reproducible.

nodes.name: Change Data Capture
nodes.what: Change data capture turns a source database's changes into a stream by reading its log, using triggers, or polling queries. Log-based CDC has the lowest impact on the source.
nodes.analogy: Subscribing to a newspaper's corrections column instead of re-reading the whole paper each day.

code.text:
# log-based CDC reads the database write-ahead log and emits row changes
# Debezium streams accounts inserts, updates, and deletes into the lakehouse

nodes.differentiator: CDC streams row-level inserts, updates, and deletes from a source so downstream systems stay current without full reloads. It turns a database's change history into a usable feed.
nodes.decisions: Using CDC to propagate account or position changes keeps analytics and risk views fresh incrementally instead of via nightly full copies. It decides how current downstream data can be.
nodes.ai_agentic: CDC keeps feature and vector stores continuously in sync with sources, so retrieval reflects the latest state. It is how AI systems avoid serving stale context.

nodes.name: Incremental View Maintenance
nodes.what: Updating a materialized view from only the changed rows instead of recomputing from scratch. Cost scales with the change size, not the table size.
nodes.analogy: Updating a running total by adding the new receipt, not re-adding every receipt.

code.text:
# maintain daily position totals from only the new trades
# new_total = prev_total + sum(changed_rows)

nodes.differentiator: Incremental view maintenance updates a materialized result from just the changed rows instead of recomputing it whole. It makes always-fresh aggregates affordable.
nodes.decisions: Maintaining an exposure rollup incrementally means each update costs a delta, not a full recompute, deciding whether a dashboard can be near-real-time. It changes the economics of freshness.
nodes.ai_agentic: Incrementally maintained features keep online serving fresh without rebuilding tables, which matters when many features update continuously. It is the efficient path to live model inputs.

nodes.name: Slowly Changing Dimensions
nodes.what: Slowly changing dimensions track attribute changes over time: Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 adds a versioned row, Type 3 keeps a prior-value column. The type chosen decides how much history survives.
nodes.analogy: Type 1 erases the old address, Type 2 keeps a dated address history, Type 3 keeps only the previous address.

code.text:
-- SCD Type 2: close the old risk_rating row and insert a new versioned row
-- keeps full history of customers.risk_rating with valid_from and valid_to

nodes.differentiator: SCD patterns record how descriptive attributes change over time, preserving history rather than overwriting it. They are what let you know what an entity looked like at a past date.
nodes.decisions: Modeling counterparty ratings or customer segments as SCD type 2 lets a report reflect the value that was true on the trade date. It is essential for correct historical analysis.
nodes.ai_agentic: Point-in-time-correct features depend on SCD history to reconstruct an entity's attributes as of a decision time. Without preserved history, models train on facts that were not yet true.

nodes.name: Bitemporal Modeling
nodes.what: Bitemporal modeling tracks valid time, when a fact was true in the world, and system time, when the system recorded it. This enables true audit and as-of reconstruction.
nodes.analogy: A ledger that records both when an event occurred and when you wrote it down, so you can ask what you believed last Tuesday.
nodes.example_note: Reinsurance fits strongly: claim reserve revisions over time
nodes.differentiator: Bitemporal modeling tracks both when something was true in the world and when the system recorded it, so corrections do not erase the past. It is the rigorous answer to restatements and audits.
nodes.decisions: Storing valid time and system time lets a firm answer both what the exposure was and what it believed at the time, which regulators often require. It makes restatements explainable rather than destructive.
nodes.ai_agentic: Reproducing a past model decision requires knowing what data the system had then, exactly what system time captures. Bitemporal data is what makes agent and model decisions defensible after the fact.

nodes.name: Object Storage Semantics
nodes.what: Object stores such as S3, GCS, and ADLS meter listing, lack atomic rename, and were historically eventually consistent. Files are immutable, so you replace rather than edit.
nodes.analogy: A mail depot where you can drop and fetch parcels but never reach in to edit one.

code.text:
# no in-place edit and no atomic rename; write a new object and swap a pointer
# listing a prefix with millions of objects is slow and metered

nodes.differentiator: Object stores offer cheap, scalable, immutable objects with weak consistency and no true rename, unlike a filesystem. Table formats exist precisely to paper over these limits, so knowing them explains the whole lakehouse stack.
nodes.decisions: Understanding that there is no atomic rename tells you why commits go through a manifest, which shapes how you design safe writes over claims or trade archives. It prevents assuming filesystem guarantees that are not there.
nodes.ai_agentic: Training and vector data live on object storage, so its semantics govern how datasets are versioned and served. The constraints here drive how AI data is laid out and committed.

nodes.name: Lakehouse Premise
nodes.what: A metadata layer brings warehouse semantics such as ACID, schema, and time travel to object-storage economics. It does so by separating the metadata layer from the file layer.
nodes.analogy: A card catalog that turns a warehouse of unmarked boxes into a queryable library.

code.text: # a metadata layer over immutable Parquet files provides ACID, schema, and time travel

nodes.differentiator: The lakehouse puts warehouse-style transactions and schemas on top of cheap object storage, so one copy serves both analytics and ML. It removes the split between a lake and a warehouse.
nodes.decisions: Adopting a lakehouse lets risk analytics and model training read the same governed tables instead of divergent copies. It decides whether the firm has one source of truth or many.
nodes.ai_agentic: A lakehouse gives AI workloads governed, transactional access to the same data analysts use, avoiding brittle exports. It is the substrate that keeps model data consistent with the business's data.

nodes.name: Iceberg Internals
nodes.what: Iceberg defines a table with a metadata tree of snapshots and manifests, supports hidden partitioning and safe schema evolution. v2 and v3 add row-level and equality deletes and deletion vectors.
nodes.analogy: A versioned table of contents that lists exactly which files make up the table right now.

code.text:
-- read the table as of an older snapshot
SELECT * FROM trades FOR SYSTEM_VERSION AS OF 8273465;

nodes.differentiator: Iceberg tracks table state through metadata, manifests, and snapshots, giving atomic commits and time travel over object storage. Its design is what makes concurrent writes and rollbacks safe on a lake.
nodes.decisions: Using Iceberg snapshots lets a team reproduce a report as of a past commit and roll back a bad write, which matters for regulated data. It turns a pile of files into an auditable table.
nodes.ai_agentic: Snapshot-based time travel lets a training run pin an exact table version for reproducibility. Iceberg's metadata is how AI datasets get versioned without copying.

nodes.name: Delta Internals
nodes.what: Delta Lake uses a transaction log of JSON commits plus Parquet checkpoints, and deletion vectors for merge-on-read deletes. UniForm exposes Iceberg-compatible metadata for the same files.
nodes.analogy: A commit log like version control, periodically snapshotted so you never replay from the beginning.

code.text:
# _delta_log holds JSON commits plus periodic Parquet checkpoints
# deletion vectors mark deleted rows without rewriting the data file

nodes.differentiator: Delta records table changes in an ordered transaction log of JSON and checkpoint files, providing ACID commits and time travel. The log is the single source of truth about the table's state.
nodes.decisions: Relying on the Delta log lets you audit exactly which commit changed a dataset and revert it, useful for claims or position tables. It makes every change traceable.
nodes.ai_agentic: The Delta log lets an AI pipeline pin and reproduce a dataset version and see its lineage of changes. Transactional history is what makes model inputs reproducible.

nodes.name: Hudi and Format Choice
nodes.what: Hudi offers copy-on-write and merge-on-read tables with a timeline of instants and record-level indexes. Choosing among Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, and Lance is a function of write pattern, ecosystem, and AI needs.
nodes.analogy: Picking a filing system by how often you revise documents versus how often you read them.

code.text:
# copy-on-write for read-heavy tables, merge-on-read for write-heavy tables
# pick Iceberg, Delta, Hudi, or Lance by write pattern, ecosystem, and AI needs

nodes.differentiator: Hudi centers on fast upserts and incremental pulls, and choosing among Hudi, Iceberg, and Delta is a real architectural decision, not a coin flip. The right format follows the workload's update and read patterns.
nodes.decisions: Picking a format by upsert rate and query pattern, Hudi for heavy streaming updates, decides how cheaply frequently-revised claims stay current. It is a deliberate fit, per table.
nodes.ai_agentic: Formats with cheap upserts and incremental reads keep feature tables fresh for online serving. Format choice quietly sets the freshness and cost of AI data.

nodes.name: Table Maintenance
nodes.what: Compaction merges small files, vacuum and snapshot expiration remove dead files, and Z-order clustering improves skipping. Unmaintained lakehouse tables degrade in both cost and speed.
nodes.analogy: Defragmenting the cabinet and shredding old drafts so it stays fast and lean.

code.text:
OPTIMIZE trades ZORDER BY (trade_ts);  -- compact small files and cluster for skipping
VACUUM trades RETAIN 168 HOURS;        -- expire dead files

nodes.differentiator: Compaction, clustering, and snapshot expiration keep a lake table fast and cheap as it accumulates small files and dead data. Skipping maintenance is how a healthy table silently degrades.
nodes.decisions: Scheduling compaction on a high-ingest surveillance table keeps scans fast and storage bounded, a direct operational choice. Neglecting it turns every query slower over time.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature and vector tables under constant writes need maintenance to keep retrieval fast and indexes tidy. Regular upkeep is what keeps AI-serving latency stable.

nodes.name: Disaggregated Storage and Compute
nodes.what: Separating storage from compute lets each scale on its own and lets compute be ephemeral. It is the defining pattern of every modern cloud data system.
nodes.analogy: Renting meeting rooms by the hour while your files live permanently in a vault.

code.text: # data lives in object storage; compute clusters spin up, read, and shut down

nodes.differentiator: Separating storage from compute lets each scale and be paid for independently, so idle compute costs nothing and storage stays cheap. It is the economic core of modern data platforms.
nodes.decisions: Disaggregation lets a firm spin compute up for month-end reserving and down afterward while data sits cheaply on object storage. It turns capacity into an on-demand decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Bursty training and batch inference map onto elastic compute over shared storage, paying only for the burst. Disaggregation is what makes spiky AI workloads affordable.

nodes.name: Pluggable Backends
nodes.what: Velox, DataFusion, Photon, and Gluten are drop-in vectorized execution layers reused across engines. They let several products share one high-performance core.
nodes.analogy: A standard engine block that several car brands bolt their own body onto.

code.text: # Velox, DataFusion, Photon, and Gluten provide a reusable vectorized execution layer

nodes.differentiator: Open table and query standards let you swap engines over the same data instead of being locked to one vendor's storage. Pluggability keeps the data layer stable while engines change.
nodes.decisions: Storing data in an open format lets a team pick the best engine per job, Trino here, Spark there, without migrating. It preserves optionality as needs evolve.
nodes.ai_agentic: AI stacks evolve fast, so open, pluggable data lets new engines and frameworks read existing tables without a rewrite. It future-proofs the data feeding models.

nodes.name: Engine Architectures
nodes.what: MPP engines like Trino and Redshift, embedded engines like DuckDB and Polars, and scale-out engines like Spark and ClickHouse suit different sizes and latencies. The right class depends on data size and concurrency, not fashion.
nodes.analogy: A fleet, a hatchback, and a freight train for different journeys.

code.text: # MPP: Trino, Redshift  |  embedded: DuckDB, Polars  |  scale-out: Spark, ClickHouse

nodes.differentiator: Query engines differ in vectorized versus compiled execution, push versus pull, and shared-nothing versus shared-disk, and these choices set their strengths. Knowing the axes lets you match engine to workload rather than follow hype.
nodes.decisions: Understanding an engine's architecture tells you whether it suits low-latency serving or heavy batch reporting on exposure data. It grounds engine selection in mechanics, not marketing.
nodes.ai_agentic: Choosing engines for feature computation and retrieval by their architecture keeps AI pipelines matched to their access patterns. The fit determines cost and latency at scale.

nodes.name: Substrait
nodes.what: Substrait is a cross-engine logical plan intermediate representation. One frontend can target many backends, and one backend can serve many frontends.
nodes.analogy: A shared blueprint format that any builder can read and construct from.

code.text: # one logical plan IR; a Polars or Spark frontend can target many execution backends

nodes.differentiator: Substrait is a cross-engine standard for serialized query plans, letting tools produce and consume the same plan format. It decouples the language and optimizer from the execution engine.
nodes.decisions: A portable plan format lets a firm move optimized logic between engines without rewriting it, protecting investment in query logic. It makes the plan an interoperable artifact.
nodes.ai_agentic: A standard plan representation gives agents and tools a checkable, portable description of the computation they request. It is a step toward machine-authored queries that run anywhere.

nodes.name: Federation
nodes.what: Federation runs one query across heterogeneous engines and sources, pushing work to each. It avoids copying data just to query it.
nodes.analogy: A general contractor coordinating specialist trades, each doing its part on site.

code.text:
-- one query joins a Postgres table and a Parquet lake table, pushing filters to each
SELECT * FROM postgres.customers c JOIN lake.payments p USING(customer_id);

nodes.differentiator: Federation queries data across multiple sources in place, avoiding copies but inheriting the slowest source's limits. It trades data movement for cross-system reach, a real tradeoff.
nodes.decisions: Federating across a warehouse and a live operational store answers a question without a pipeline, but you must weigh latency and load on the source. It decides when to move data versus reach into it.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agents often need context from several systems, and federation offers a single access path across them. Its cost profile decides when to federate versus pre-stage the data.

nodes.name: Memory Budgets
nodes.what: Per-operator memory accounting decides whether a query spills or fails. On-heap versus off-heap placement changes garbage-collection behavior under load.
nodes.analogy: Each department gets a budget; overspending triggers a spill to a cheaper option, not bankruptcy.

code.text: spark.conf.set("spark.memory.fraction", "0.6")  # operator budget; overflow spills, not crashes

nodes.differentiator: Every operator competes for finite memory, and a job that ignores its budget spills or fails under load. Treating memory as a budget to allocate is what keeps large jobs stable.
nodes.decisions: Sizing partitions and operators to the memory budget decides whether a large exposure aggregation runs smoothly or thrashes. It is a capacity decision made before the job, not after it fails.
nodes.ai_agentic: Training and batch inference are memory-bound, so explicit budgets keep GPU and host memory from overflowing mid-run. Managing the budget keeps large AI jobs from crashing.

nodes.name: Backpressure and Admission Control
nodes.what: Backpressure slows producers when consumers fall behind; admission control queues or rejects new work to protect SLAs. Both bound the work in flight.
nodes.analogy: A busy restaurant pacing the kitchen and pausing the waitlist rather than seating everyone at once.

code.text: # slow producers when the sink lags; queue or reject new queries to protect SLAs

nodes.differentiator: Backpressure slows producers when consumers fall behind, and admission control refuses work the system cannot serve, protecting stability. Together they keep a system from collapsing under overload.
nodes.decisions: Applying admission control to a surveillance ingest pipeline keeps a spike from taking down the whole system, a deliberate reliability choice. It decides how the system behaves at its limits.
nodes.ai_agentic: Serving many concurrent agent and retrieval requests needs backpressure and admission control to stay responsive under bursts. It is what keeps an AI service stable when demand spikes.

nodes.name: Schedulers and Autoscaling
nodes.what: YARN and Kubernetes allocate resources; autoscaling adds or removes capacity reactively or predictively. The policy trades dollar cost against latency.
nodes.analogy: Calling in more staff when the queue grows and sending them home when it shrinks.

code.text: # Kubernetes allocates executors; dynamic allocation adds and removes them with load

nodes.differentiator: Schedulers place work and autoscalers add or remove capacity to match load, turning fixed clusters into elastic ones. Good policies keep both cost and latency in check.
nodes.decisions: Autoscaling compute for month-end batch and scaling down after keeps spend aligned with actual demand. Scheduler and scaling policy is a direct cost-versus-latency decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Spiky training and inference loads depend on autoscaling to meet demand without paying for idle GPUs. Scheduling policy governs the cost of elastic AI workloads.

nodes.name: Multi-Tenancy and Isolation
nodes.what: Resource queues, namespaces, and concurrency limits stop one tenant's heavy job from starving others. This is the cure for the noisy neighbor problem.
nodes.analogy: Separate lanes on a shared road so one truck does not block every car.

code.text: # separate resource queues per team stop one heavy job from starving the others

nodes.differentiator: Multi-tenancy shares infrastructure across teams, and isolation stops one tenant's heavy job from starving others. Without isolation, a shared platform is one bad query from an outage.
nodes.decisions: Enforcing resource isolation lets a trading desk's ad hoc query not degrade the firm's regulatory reporting on the same cluster. It decides whether sharing is safe.
nodes.ai_agentic: Shared model-serving and data platforms need isolation so one tenant's load does not degrade another's latency. It keeps a multi-team AI platform predictable.

nodes.name: Data Lineage
nodes.what: Dataset-level and column-level data lineage records where data came from and what it feeds. It enables impact analysis and faster debugging.
nodes.analogy: A supply-chain label tracing every ingredient back to its farm.

code.text:
# emit OpenLineage events so each dataset records its inputs and consumers
# column-level lineage shows report.total derives from payments.amount

nodes.differentiator: Lineage records where data came from and how it was transformed, making impact analysis and root-cause possible. It is what lets you answer which report a bad upstream change affects.
nodes.decisions: Lineage lets a team trace a wrong figure in a regulatory report back to its source column and fix the cause, not the symptom. It turns debugging and audits into tracing.
nodes.ai_agentic: When a model or agent produces a bad output, lineage traces it to the features and sources responsible. It is essential for debugging and governing AI systems.

nodes.name: Schema Evolution
nodes.what: Forward, backward, and full compatibility rules govern safe schema change. The wrong change silently breaks consumers downstream.
nodes.analogy: Updating a form so that both old and new printed copies remain readable.

code.text: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment STRING;  -- a nullable add is backward compatible

nodes.differentiator: Schema evolution lets tables add, drop, or change columns safely over time without breaking readers. Handling it deliberately prevents a schema change from silently breaking pipelines.
nodes.decisions: Adopting compatible evolution rules lets a claims schema grow without rewriting history or breaking downstream reports. It decides whether change is smooth or a migration crisis.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature schemas change as models evolve, so safe evolution keeps training and serving from drifting apart. Compatibility rules protect the pipelines that feed models.

nodes.name: Data Contracts
nodes.what: A data contract is a producer-consumer agreement with an explicit schema, semantics, and SLA. It is enforced in CI so a breaking change fails the build.
nodes.analogy: A delivery contract specifying size, timing, and quality, signed by both sides.

code.text: # the producer of payments commits to a schema, freshness SLA, and semantics; CI checks it

nodes.differentiator: A data contract is an explicit, enforced agreement on schema and semantics between producer and consumer. It moves data quality upstream to where breakage originates.
nodes.decisions: A contract on an upstream trade feed makes a breaking change fail loudly at the source instead of silently corrupting reports. It decides where errors surface, early or late.
nodes.ai_agentic: Contracts on feature and source data give agents and models a stable, guaranteed interface to depend on. They are what make automated data consumption safe.

nodes.name: Data Quality
nodes.what: Frameworks like Great Expectations, Soda, and dbt tests assert row counts, ranges, and uniqueness. They act as a gate that stops bad data from propagating.
nodes.analogy: Quality-control sampling on a production line that halts the belt on a defect.

code.text:
# Great Expectations: assert amount is non-negative and customer_id is present
expect_column_values_to_be_between("amount", min_value=0, max_value=None)

nodes.differentiator: Data quality checks for completeness, validity, freshness, and uniqueness catch bad data before it reaches decisions. Codifying them turns quality from hope into an enforced gate.
nodes.decisions: Quality gates on reserving inputs stop a null-riddled feed from producing a confidently wrong number. They decide whether a downstream decision can be trusted.
nodes.ai_agentic: Models and agents amplify bad data quietly, so quality gates on their inputs are the first line of defense. Enforced checks keep AI outputs from inheriting silent errors.

nodes.name: Testing for Data
nodes.what: Unit tests on pure transforms, property-based testing, snapshot testing, and data diffing catch regressions before release. Pipelines become testable when transforms are pure functions.
nodes.analogy: A test suite plus a before-and-after photo comparison for every change.

code.text:
# unit test a pure transform on a tiny banking fixture
assert normalize_currency("gbp") == "GBP"

nodes.differentiator: Testing pipelines with unit, integration, and expectation checks catches logic and data errors before production. It brings software discipline to data engineering.
nodes.decisions: Testing a transformation against known cases means a change to an exposure calculation is verified before it ships. It decides whether pipeline changes are safe to deploy.
nodes.ai_agentic: Automated data tests give agents and generated pipelines a safety net that catches regressions before they reach models. Tests are what make machine-authored data changes trustworthy.

nodes.name: Catalog as Policy
nodes.what: The catalog above the engines is the natural place to enforce access, since every engine consults it. Policy lives in one place rather than in each application.
nodes.analogy: One staffed gate to the building instead of a separate lock on every interior door.

code.text: GRANT SELECT ON payments TO ROLE analyst_emea;  -- enforced at the catalog, every engine obeys

nodes.differentiator: A modern catalog is not just a table list but the enforcement point for access, governance, and lineage policy. Treating the catalog as policy centralizes control that would otherwise scatter.
nodes.decisions: Centralizing access rules in the catalog lets the firm govern who sees which trades or PII in one place, not per engine. It decides whether governance is consistent or ad hoc.
nodes.ai_agentic: As agents query data autonomously, catalog-enforced policy keeps their access within bounds. It is the control plane that governs machine access at scale.

nodes.name: Row and Column Security
nodes.what: Row-level security and column-level security restrict which rows and columns a principal can see. Enforcement sits at the catalog or engine layer.
nodes.analogy: A redacted document where your clearance decides which lines and pages appear.
nodes.example_note: Banking: analysts see only their region's accounts

code.text:
-- analysts see only rows for their own branches
CREATE ROW FILTER region_filter ON accounts AS (branch_id IN current_user_branches());

nodes.differentiator: Row and column security restricts data at the cell level so different users see different slices of the same table. It enforces need-to-know without duplicating data.
nodes.decisions: Applying row filters by desk and column masks on PII lets one governed table serve many roles safely. It decides how finely access can be controlled.
nodes.ai_agentic: Fine-grained security must follow data into retrieval so an agent only surfaces what the user is entitled to see. It is essential to prevent AI systems from leaking restricted rows.

nodes.name: Masking and Tokenization
nodes.what: Masking irreversibly obscures a value; tokenization swaps it for a reversible token held in a vault. Both protect sensitive banking fields such as PII and card numbers.
nodes.analogy: Blacking out a number versus replacing it with a claim-check stub you can later redeem.

code.text: # masking blanks the card number to XXXX; tokenization swaps it for a reversible vault token

nodes.differentiator: Masking hides sensitive values and tokenization replaces them with reversible surrogates, protecting data while keeping it usable. They let analytics proceed without exposing raw PII.
nodes.decisions: Tokenizing account numbers lets analysts join and aggregate without ever seeing the real identifiers, meeting privacy rules. It decides how sensitive data can be used safely.
nodes.ai_agentic: Masking and tokenization keep PII out of prompts, embeddings, and logs while preserving analytic utility. They let AI pipelines use sensitive data without leaking it.

nodes.name: Encryption
nodes.what: Encryption at rest and in transit with envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key, plus key rotation. It protects data even when storage or network is compromised.
nodes.analogy: A locked container plus a master key you control and can change at will.

code.text: # envelope encryption: a data key encrypts data, a master key (BYOK) encrypts the data key

nodes.differentiator: Encryption at rest and in transit, with managed keys, protects data even if storage or network is compromised. It is the baseline control regulators and clients expect.
nodes.decisions: Enforcing encryption and key management on financial data is a compliance requirement that shapes storage and access design. It decides whether the platform meets its obligations.
nodes.ai_agentic: Training data, embeddings, and model inputs are sensitive and must be encrypted along the whole AI pipeline. Key management extends the same guarantees to AI artifacts.

nodes.name: Cost Units
nodes.what: Reason in dollars per TB scanned, per query, and per GB stored as first-class design constraints. These units, not finance trivia, drive layout and pruning choices.
nodes.analogy: Pricing a journey by fuel per mile before choosing the route.

code.text:
-- a serverless engine bills by bytes scanned; pruning columns and partitions cuts the bill
SELECT trade_id, price FROM trades WHERE trade_date = DATE '2025-06-01';

nodes.differentiator: Understanding the true unit of cost, bytes scanned, compute-seconds, requests, lets you optimize the thing that actually drives the bill. Optimizing the wrong unit wastes effort.
nodes.decisions: Knowing a query is billed by bytes scanned tells you to prune and partition rather than tune compute. It focuses optimization on the real cost driver.
nodes.ai_agentic: AI workloads bill in tokens, GPU-hours, and vector queries, so knowing the unit is what makes cost control effective. Optimizing the right unit keeps AI spend sane.

nodes.name: Storage Tiering
nodes.what: Hot, warm, cold, and archive tiers trade retrieval speed for storage price. Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.
nodes.analogy: Desk drawer, filing cabinet, basement, and off-site vault for how often you reach for it.
nodes.example_note: Reinsurance: old claims age into archive storage

code.text: # lifecycle policy moves claims older than 2 years from hot to archive storage

nodes.differentiator: Tiering moves data across hot, warm, and cold storage by access frequency, matching cost to value. It keeps rarely-read history cheap without deleting it.
nodes.decisions: Tiering old trade and claims archives to cold storage cuts cost while keeping data available for audits. It decides the ongoing cost of retained history.
nodes.ai_agentic: Cold training data and old embeddings can sit in cheap tiers while hot features stay fast, balancing AI storage cost. Tiering keeps large AI corpora affordable to retain.

nodes.name: Compute Purchasing
nodes.what: Spot, on-demand, and reserved capacity trade price against reliability and commitment. The mix should match how interruptible each workload is.
nodes.analogy: Standby tickets, walk-up fares, and a season pass for different travel needs.

code.text: # spot for fault-tolerant batch, reserved for steady baseline, on-demand for spikes

nodes.differentiator: Choosing among on-demand, reserved, and spot compute trades price against reliability and flexibility. The right mix can cut cost substantially for the same work.
nodes.decisions: Running interruptible batch reserving on spot and critical reporting on reserved capacity matches purchase type to tolerance for failure. It is a direct cost decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Fault-tolerant training can exploit cheap spot GPUs while latency-critical serving uses reserved capacity. Purchasing strategy is a major lever on AI compute cost.

nodes.name: Cache vs Recompute
nodes.what: Caching trades storage and staleness risk for repeated-query speed. Sometimes recomputing is cheaper than maintaining a cache.
nodes.analogy: Keeping leftovers versus cooking fresh, depending on how often you eat the dish.

code.text: # cache a daily aggregate if it is queried often; recompute if rarely read or cheap to derive

nodes.differentiator: Caching a result trades storage and staleness risk against the cost of recomputing it, and the right call depends on read frequency and volatility. It is a deliberate economic tradeoff, not a default.
nodes.decisions: Caching a stable, frequently-read exposure aggregate saves repeated computation, while volatile data is better recomputed. It decides where to spend compute versus storage.
nodes.ai_agentic: Caching embeddings and retrieval results avoids recomputing them per request, cutting latency and cost for repeated queries. Deciding what to cache is central to efficient AI serving.

nodes.name: Embeddings as Data
nodes.what: An embedding is a learned dense vector that represents an item's meaning. It is a first-class data type whose access pattern is similarity, not equality.
nodes.analogy: Placing every document on a map so that related ones sit near each other.

code.text:
# an embedding is a dense vector; store it next to the row it represents
vec = embed("counterparty due diligence note")  # shape (1024,)
