nodes.differentiator: Embeddings are just high-dimensional numeric columns and deserve the same engineering as any data, versioning, lineage, and layout. Treating them as first-class data, not model exhaust, keeps them maintainable.
nodes.decisions: Versioning embeddings and tracking which model produced them lets you reason about drift and reindex deliberately. It decides whether a vector store stays trustworthy over time.
nodes.ai_agentic: Every RAG and agent-memory system rests on embeddings, so managing them as governed data is foundational. Their quality and freshness directly bound retrieval quality.

nodes.name: Vector Indexes
nodes.what: HNSW is a navigable graph, IVF and IVF-PQ partition then search, and DiskANN and ScaNN serve billion-scale corpora from disk. Each exposes the recall, latency, and build-cost triangle.
nodes.analogy: Neighborhood maps and shortcuts so you find nearby points without checking the whole city.

code.text: # HNSW: graph of nearest neighbors  |  IVF and IVF-PQ: cluster then search  |  DiskANN: on disk

nodes.differentiator: Vector indexes like HNSW and IVF make similarity search fast by trading exactness and build cost for query speed. Choosing and tuning the index sets retrieval latency and recall.
nodes.decisions: Picking an index and its parameters lets you hit a target recall at a latency budget for a similarity lookup. It is a deliberate accuracy-versus-speed decision.
nodes.ai_agentic: Vector indexes are the retrieval engine of RAG and agent memory, so their tuning bounds how good and how fast context assembly is. They are core AI infrastructure, not an afterthought.

nodes.name: Vector Storage
nodes.what: Dedicated stores such as Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, and Qdrant, extensions such as pgvector and Elasticsearch, and Lance and LanceDB keep vectors near the data. The choice trades operational simplicity against unification with analytical columns.
nodes.analogy: A specialty library wing versus adding a vector shelf to the existing library.

code.text:
# Lance stores vectors and columns together; query by similarity
tbl.search(query_vec).limit(10).to_arrow()

nodes.differentiator: Storing vectors well means handling their size, layout, and metadata alongside filters, not just dumping arrays. Good vector storage supports filtered, scalable similarity search.
nodes.decisions: Designing vector storage with the right metadata and partitioning lets a retrieval filter by entity or date before searching. It decides whether retrieval can be both relevant and fast.
nodes.ai_agentic: Vector storage is the substrate for retrieval, so its design sets the ceiling on RAG performance and cost. Filterable, well-laid-out vectors are what make agent retrieval precise.

nodes.name: Retrieval Modes
nodes.what: Sparse retrieval with BM25 over an inverted index matches terms; dense retrieval matches embeddings; hybrid search blends both with a reranker. The mix is chosen for recall and precision needs.
nodes.analogy: Keyword search, meaning search, and a judge who blends the two shortlists.

code.text: # sparse: BM25 over an inverted index  |  dense: embedding similarity  |  hybrid: blend + rerank

nodes.differentiator: Retrieval can be dense, sparse, or hybrid, and each suits different queries, with hybrid often winning on real corpora. Knowing the modes lets you match retrieval to the question.
nodes.decisions: Combining keyword and semantic retrieval for a policy or filings search catches both exact terms and meaning. Choosing the mode decides what the system can find.
nodes.ai_agentic: Retrieval mode directly determines what context an agent receives, and thus the quality of its answers. Hybrid retrieval is often the difference between grounded and hallucinated responses.

nodes.name: RAG as a Workload
nodes.what: RAG is a data pipeline: parse and chunk documents, index them, filter by metadata, keep fresh, and evaluate. It is data engineering, not a model trick.
nodes.analogy: Running a research desk that files sources, retrieves the right ones on demand, and audits its hit rate.
related: evaluation such as recall at k and MRR

code.text: # parse -> chunk -> embed -> index -> retrieve with metadata filter -> evaluate recall at k

nodes.differentiator: RAG is a data workload, embed, index, retrieve, rank, as much as a model one, and its quality is bounded by the pipeline behind it. Treating it as a workload is what makes it improvable.
nodes.decisions: Viewing RAG as a pipeline lets you fix retrieval quality with better chunking, filtering, and freshness rather than only prompt tweaks. It decides where to invest to improve answers.
nodes.ai_agentic: RAG is the backbone of grounded agents, and its data engineering, not the LLM alone, sets the reliability of their answers. Strong retrieval is what keeps agents factual.

nodes.name: Feature Stores
nodes.what: A feature store serves the same feature definitions online at low latency and offline in batch. This avoids online-offline skew between training and serving.
nodes.analogy: One recipe used in both the test kitchen and the restaurant so the dish never differs.
nodes.example_note: Banking: fraud features computed identically at scoring and training time

code.text: # define a fraud feature once; serve it online for scoring and offline for training

nodes.differentiator: A feature store centralizes feature definitions and serves them consistently to training and inference, preventing train-serve skew. It keeps a model seeing the same feature offline and online.
nodes.decisions: Sharing governed features across credit and fraud models avoids each team re-deriving them inconsistently. It decides whether feature logic is reused or silently diverges.
nodes.ai_agentic: Feature stores give agents and models consistent, fresh, point-in-time-correct inputs from one place. They are core infrastructure for reliable, reproducible AI decisions.

nodes.name: Point-in-Time Correctness
nodes.what: Assemble training data using only information available as of the label time. This avoids label leakage that inflates offline metrics.
nodes.analogy: Grading a forecast using only what was known before the event, never after.

code.text:
-- as-of join: attach only feature values known before the label timestamp
SELECT * FROM labels l ASOF JOIN features f ON f.entity = l.entity AND f.ts <= l.label_ts;

nodes.differentiator: Joining features as of the decision time, not as of now, is the line between an honest backtest and one poisoned by leakage. The flaw is invisible in the schema and catches teams that treat a feature table like a current-state table.
nodes.decisions: As-of joins let a credit or underwriting model be scored on exactly what was known when the application arrived, so measured performance matches production. Without it, approval and pricing decisions rest on inflated offline metrics.
nodes.ai_agentic: Agentic systems that assemble features or retrieve records on the fly must reconstruct the state at the relevant timestamp, or they reason over facts that did not yet exist. Point-in-time correctness is what makes retrieved context trustworthy for a decision.

nodes.name: Data Loader as a System
nodes.what: The data loader is a CPU-to-GPU pipeline with workers, prefetch queues, and shared memory. It must hide I/O behind compute or the accelerator stalls.
nodes.analogy: A pit crew handing over the next tire before the car stops, so the engine never waits.

code.text:
# overlap I/O with compute so the GPU never waits
DataLoader(ds, num_workers=8, prefetch_factor=4, pin_memory=True)

nodes.differentiator: The training data loader is a real system, shuffling, batching, prefetching, that can bottleneck an expensive GPU if built naively. Treating it as infrastructure keeps accelerators fed.
nodes.decisions: Engineering the loader to prefetch and stream keeps a costly GPU from idling on I/O, a direct utilization decision. It determines how much of paid compute is actually used.
nodes.ai_agentic: As training and fine-tuning scale, the loader often decides throughput and cost more than the model code. It is where data engineering directly meets AI economics.

nodes.name: Sharding and Streaming Datasets
nodes.what: File-level sharding and streaming formats such as WebDataset, MosaicML Streaming, and Lance stream training data from object storage. They avoid hot spots across many GPUs.
nodes.analogy: Dealing cards evenly from several decks so no single dealer is overworked.

code.text: # shard files evenly and stream from object storage with WebDataset, Mosaic, or Lance

nodes.differentiator: Datasets too large to fit are sharded and streamed so training reads them incrementally without loading everything. It is what makes training on enormous corpora feasible.
nodes.decisions: Sharding a huge training corpus with balanced, streamable partitions decides whether a run is I/O-bound or smooth. It is a layout choice that governs training throughput.
nodes.ai_agentic: Frontier-scale training depends on sharded, streamed pipelines to feed compute continuously. This layout is a prerequisite for large AI workloads, not an optimization.

nodes.name: GPU-Aware Formats
nodes.what: Random access on Parquet stalls training, so Lance and tfrecord shards exist for sequential and shardable reads. GPUDirect Storage loads data directly into device memory.
nodes.analogy: A conveyor that drops parts straight onto the assembly arm instead of routing through a stockroom.

code.text: # random reads on Parquet stall training; Lance and tfrecord shards plus GPUDirect load fast

nodes.differentiator: GPU-aware formats and direct paths get data into accelerator memory with minimal CPU copying and conversion. They remove the host bottleneck between storage and the GPU.
nodes.decisions: Choosing a GPU-friendly format and load path decides whether accelerators run near capacity or wait on the CPU. It is a concrete lever on training and inference throughput.
nodes.ai_agentic: As AI workloads grow, feeding GPUs efficiently from storage becomes a central data-engineering problem. GPU-aware formats are what keep expensive accelerators busy.
